name: Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts

facts.text: Is the longest continuously operating art museum and art school in the United States.
Was founded by painter Charles Willson Peale, sculptor William Rush and other artists and business leaders.
The current building was designed by Frank Furness and George Hewitt, begun in 1871 and opened in 1876.
Shows contemporary art by established international artists alongside young talent.
Was established in 1915 as a multidisciplinary center for visual, literary and performing arts.
Is housed in the Wetherill mansion, designed in 1906 by Frank Miles Day.
Became part of the University of the Arts in 2017.
The building was purchased by the Curtis Institute of Music after the University of the Arts closed in 2024.
Was founded in 1988 by collector Barbara Whiteman.
Emphasizes the collection and preservation of black dolls as artifacts of history and culture.
Holds a permanent collection of approximately 1,000 dolls, ranging from small figurines to full-size figures.
Occupies the former Finney & Son mausoleum showroom, a building dating to 1865.
Was established in September 2010 by Gavin Hecker.
The building was bought by the music producer Diplo in the mid-2000s as headquarters of his Mad Decent label.
Was founded in 1975 and is located within Congregation Rodeph Shalom.
Exhibits contemporary art that illuminates the Jewish experience.
Its permanent collection includes works by Chaim Gross, Tobi Kahn, Joan Snyder and Roman Vishniac.
Built from 1785 to 1789 as the headquarters of the American Philosophical Society.
Is the only privately owned structure on Independence Square.
A loan from society member Benjamin Franklin provided the final money needed to finish construction.
Opened to the public in 2001 as the American Philosophical Society Museum.
Began when Montessori educator Portia Sperr gathered a group of families to create a hands-on museum for young children.
Its pilot program opened October 2, 1976, in 2,200 square feet at the Academy of Natural Sciences.
Moved to Cherry Street in 1978 and bought a three-story building on North 21st Street in 1983.

name: Portrait Gallery in the Second Bank

facts.text: Houses a permanent collection of more than 150 portraits of founders and other leaders of the early republic.
More than 100 portraits by Charles Willson Peale form the core of the collection.
Occupies a Greek Revival building designed by William Strickland and built between 1819 and 1824.
Was built in 1765 in the Georgian style.
Samuel Powel bought the newly built house in 1769 from merchant Charles Stedman.
Powel was the last mayor of Philadelphia under the British Crown and the first mayor under the new charter in 1789.
Is managed by the Philadelphia Society for the Preservation of Landmarks.
Was organized on May 20, 1852, at the General Assembly meeting in Charleston, South Carolina.
Holds about 32,000 cubic feet of archival records and personal papers.
Its museum collection includes about 250 paintings and over 25,000 communion tokens.
Has been headquartered in the Finley House since 1948, when owner Dorothy Finley offered the basement kitchen.
The kitchen, built in 1789, is the core of the former farmhouse of Captain John Pugh, a Revolutionary War veteran.
Miss Finley gave the rest of the house to the society in 1964.
Dates to 1707 and is the birthplace of astronomer David Rittenhouse.
Papermaker William Rittenhouse built the first paper mill in British North America nearby with his son Nicholas.
Is a National Historic Landmark in Historic Rittenhouse Town, beside Paper Mill Run.
Holds one of the largest collections of Auguste Rodin's works outside Paris.
Was a gift to the city from movie-theatre magnate Jules Mastbaum, who began collecting Rodin in 1923.
Architects Paul Cret and Jacques Greber designed the building and gardens.
Is administered by the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
Director Rodica Perciali has assembled about a thousand eggs hand-decorated by Romanian artisans.
Displays four large ostrich eggs among the decorated eggs.
Also shows costumes, furniture, rugs, glassware, pottery and a collage on the history of Romanian immigration.
Occupies four buildings that were the Church of the Evangelists and St. Martin's College for Indigent Boys.
The campanile dates to 1857, the basilica to 1884-1886 and St. Martin's College to 1906.
Samuel S. Fleisher bought the church in 1922 and converted it into an art gallery.
Is home to the Graphic Sketch Club, founded by Samuel S. Fleisher.

name: Schuylkill Center for Environmental Education Visitor Center

facts.text: The Schuylkill Center was founded in 1965 as Philadelphia's first environmental education center.
The center's grounds cover 365 acres of fields and forests.
Was founded in 1982 as the Center for the History of Chemistry, a venture of the American Chemical Society and Penn.
Occupies the 1866 First National Bank building, bought in 1995, and moved in on February 1, 1996.
Was known as the Chemical Heritage Foundation until it was renamed in 2018.
Is a child-centered art studio in Narberth with classes in drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture and textile dyeing.
Runs after-school programs, spring and summer art camps, Saturday workshops and art parties.
Features the abstract expressionist work of resident artist Diane E. Vaughn.

name: St. George's United Methodist Church House Museum and Library

facts.text: The congregation was founded in 1767 and first met in a sail loft on Dock Street.
In 1769 it bought the shell of a building erected in 1763 by a German Reformed congregation.
Is the oldest Methodist church in continuous use in the United States.
Is part of the Rutgers-Camden Center for the Arts, in the Fine Arts Complex on the Rutgers-Camden campus.
Held a 50th anniversary show titled Emerging.
Was built between 1783 and 1789 as a summer home by Judge William Lewis and originally named Summerville.
Joseph Hemphill bought it in 1821, and his family added Greek Revival wings around 1828.
Got its current name between 1846 and 1867, believed to come from farmers who served strawberries and cream.
Preserves the boarding house at 3rd and Pine Streets where Kosciuszko stayed after returning to America in 1797.
Was authorized as a national memorial on October 21, 1972.
At 0.02 acres, is the smallest unit of the National Park System.
Was founded in 2015 by Vashti Dubois.
Is a memoir museum devoted to the stories and history of ordinary Black girls and women.
Is housed in a Victorian twin home in Germantown.
Was founded in 1731 by Benjamin Franklin and fellow members of the Junto discussion group.
Its Locust Street building, the Ridgway Library, was completed in 1965 and opened to the public in April 1966.
Is a non-profit organization.

name: The Mario Lanza Institute and Museum

facts.text: Occupies a renovated East Passyunk storage garage that Bill Ronayne first saw in 2018.
Stands at 12th and Reed Streets, across from the Columbus Square Dog Park.
Offers artist studios in a renovated historic factory building in Kensington.

name: The Philadelphia Masonic Temple, Library and Museum

facts.text: Exterior designed by James H. Windrim; interior designed by George Herzog.
The ten-ton granite cornerstone was laid on June 24, 1868, and the temple was dedicated September 29, 1873.
Is the headquarters of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania and has seven lodge rooms.
Was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1985.
Was founded in 1915 as The Print Club of Philadelphia by art collectors and artists.
Moved in 1918 to a late 19th century carriage house at 1614 Latimer Street.
Established its Annual International Competition in 1924.
